heroes.headline: DJI Mini 5 Pro: The Best Sub-250g Drone You Can (Still) Buy in America
heroes.one_liner: DJI's best pocket drone: a 1-inch 50MP sensor and LiDAR night-sensing in a 249g body — but DJI never officially sold it in the US.
heroes.story: Launched September 18, 2025, the DJI Mini 5 Pro packs a 1-inch 50MP CMOS sensor, 4K/60 HDR video, a 225-degree flexible gimbal, forward LiDAR and omnidirectional obstacle sensing into a 249g body that stays under the registration threshold in most countries. It is, on image quality per gram, the best small camera drone on the market. The catch for Americans: DJI never listed the Mini 5 Pro (or the flagship Mavic 4 Pro) on its US store, blaming a 'customs misunderstanding,' though authorized dealers like B&H stock it. On December 22, 2025 the FCC added all DJI gear to its Covered List, so no NEW DJI models can get fresh US authorization going forward — but existing units keep flying and the FCC extended security/firmware updates to January 1, 2029.
heroes.founding_story: DJI (Da-Jiang Innovations) was founded November 6, 2006 by Frank Wang (Wang Tao), then a student at the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, who prototyped flight controllers in his dorm before moving the company to Shenzhen. It bootstrapped from selling ~$6,000 flight-control modules into the dominant global drone maker (roughly 70%+ consumer share) via the Phantom and later Mavic and Mini lines. The Mini series (since the 2019 Mavic Mini) exists specifically to slip under the sub-250g regulatory line.
heroes.who_should_use: Travel vloggers and YouTubers, real-estate and property photographers, hobbyists and casual creators who want near-professional aerial stills and video without registration paperwork, and anyone who values a drone that fits in a jacket pocket.
heroes.who_should_buy: Buy it if you want the best-imaging pocket drone, period — roughly $800 for the base kit and about $1,100-1,400 for the Fly More combo through US authorized dealers. What is genuinely special: a true 1-inch sensor, vertical/225-degree gimbal and LiDAR low-light avoidance at 249g is unmatched. Who should NOT: US buyers who need DJI's official US warranty channel, who worry about long-term parts/repair availability under the ban, or anyone doing federal/law-enforcement work (DJI is locked out of that procurement).
heroes.free_alternatives: The older DJI Mini 4 Pro is cheaper, still excellent, and gives you ~90% of the Mini 5 Pro with a smaller sensor. The DJI Neo / Neo 2 (~$199) is far cheaper but a tiny-sensor selfie drone, not a photo tool. HoverAir X1 is a self-flying alternative but no 1-inch sensor. Autel's Nano/Lite compete but are also now on the Covered List. Honestly: for pure image quality nothing cheaper beats the 1-inch sensor, but the Mini 4 Pro is the value pick.
heroes.verdict: BUY — the best pocket drone made, but buy from a US authorized dealer now; the ban means supply, parts and support only get harder from here.

heroes.headline: Skydio X10D Lands the Largest Single-Vendor Drone Order in US Army History
heroes.one_liner: The American anti-DJI just won a $52M, ~3,000-unit US Army order — the biggest single-vendor sUAS buy in Army history, awarded in 72 hours.
heroes.story: In March 2026 the US Army ordered nearly 3,000 Skydio X10D drones for more than $52 million — the largest single-vendor small-UAS purchase in Army history, and notably moved from bid to award in under 72 hours. The X10D is the defense variant of the X10, built for GPS-denied, electronically-contested airspace using six navigation cameras and visual inertial odometry to hold position and navigate home when satellite signals are jammed or spoofed. It carries 48MP telephoto, 50.3MP wide and 64MP narrow cameras plus the first Teledyne FLIR Boson+ thermal (640x512) on a small UAS. In April 2026 Skydio added a ~$9M USAFCENT contract to secure US airbases in the Middle East.
heroes.founding_story: Skydio was founded in 2014 by Adam Bry, Abe Bachrach and Matt Donahoe, MIT alumni who had worked on Google's Project Wing. It first made its name with self-flying consumer drones (R1, Skydio 2), then in August 2023 made the 'very difficult decision' to exit the consumer market entirely — it was losing money on every consumer unit — to focus on enterprise and public safety. It is now the largest US drone maker, with over 1,500 enterprise/public-sector customers and more than half its business in defense (reportedly ~22,000 units with the DoD).
heroes.who_should_use: Police and fire departments running drone-as-first-responder programs, utility/rail/pipeline inspectors, the military for ISR, base and border security teams, and search-and-rescue units — anyone who needs a drone that keeps flying when GPS is jammed.
heroes.who_should_buy: Government agencies and enterprises that need NDAA-compliant, US-made autonomy. Price reality: Skydio does not publish prices; enterprise X10 packages run well into five figures (roughly $11k and up) and X10D defense kits higher, usually bundled with subscriptions and support. What is genuinely special is the best-in-class obstacle-dodging autonomy and true GPS-denied navigation. Who should NOT: consumers and hobbyists — you effectively cannot buy one, and it is wildly overkill and overpriced next to a DJI Mini.
heroes.free_alternatives: For agencies, DJI's Matrice line is cheaper and arguably more capable per dollar — but banned from federal and most government use, which is the whole point of Skydio. In public safety, BRINC, Flock's Alpha and Autel (also Covered-Listed) compete. For consumers there is simply no reason to consider Skydio; a DJI Mini or Air wins on price and image quality.
heroes.verdict: USE — if you need NDAA-compliant US autonomy in contested airspace it is the leader; everyone else, skip — it is not for you and not for sale to you.

heroes.headline: Amazon Prime Air Drone Delivery Is Finally Real — and Coming to a Suburb Near You
heroes.one_liner: MK30 drones now drop sub-5-lb packages in ~30 minutes across a dozen-plus US metros — $4.99 for Prime members, if you live in a covered suburb.
heroes.story: Amazon's MK30 drone (an ~83-lb aircraft that carries up to 5 lb at ~73 mph within a 7.5-mile radius, and flies in light rain) is now live or announced across Texas (San Antonio, Waco, Dallas-Fort Worth, a Houston site), Arizona (Tolleson), the Detroit suburbs, Tampa, Kansas City, Baton Rouge, Chicago's south suburbs and the Omaha suburbs, with metro Atlanta being explored. The service had made roughly 16,000 deliveries by early 2026. Amazon says it will reach communities with 30 million customers by the end of 2026 and 500 million annual deliveries by 2030. Pricing runs $4.99 per delivery for Prime members and $9.99 for non-members.
heroes.founding_story: Jeff Bezos unveiled Prime Air on 60 Minutes in December 2013 with a '30-minute delivery' promise that was widely mocked as vaporware. It took more than nine years, several drone redesigns and a modest 2022 debut in Lockeford, California and College Station, Texas before the service reached real neighborhoods at any scale. Rivals got to routine autonomous flight first: Alphabet's Wing (spun out of Google X in 2018) and Zipline (founded 2014 by Keller Rinaudo Cliffton, which cut its teeth delivering blood and medicine in Rwanda and Ghana).
heroes.who_should_use: Suburban Prime members in covered zones who occasionally need small, urgent items fast — medications, batteries, a phone charger, small household goods — and who have a clear yard or drop space for the drone.
heroes.who_should_buy: It costs nothing to try if you are in a coverage area and it is genuinely fast for light, urgent items. The honest reality: it only carries items under 5 lb, needs open drop space, the eligible catalog is limited, and it is weather- and daylight-limited. Who should NOT bother: apartment dwellers, rural customers (not covered), and the ~99% of people who simply do not live in one of the narrow launch suburbs yet.
heroes.free_alternatives: For most people, standard Prime same-day/next-day delivery is free (with membership), needs no yard, and carries any size item — it beats drones today for nearly everything. Where available, Walmart's Wing partnership and Zipline do the same job; DoorDash/Instacart cover urgent convenience items; and your local pharmacy still wins for a single prescription.
heroes.verdict: USE — genuinely quick and effectively free for Prime members in coverage; for everyone else it is still a tech demo, not a service you can rely on.

heroes.headline: FAA's Part 108 BVLOS Rule: The Regulation That Unlocks the Whole US Drone Economy — Still Not Final
heroes.one_liner: The rule to make routine beyond-visual-line-of-sight flights legal at scale — the key to delivery and inspection — is still not final in mid-2026.
heroes.story: Part 108 would replace the slow, per-flight Part 107 waiver regime with a standardized framework for routine Beyond Visual Line of Sight operations — the thing that makes drone delivery, long-range infrastructure inspection and drone-as-first-responder economically viable — for aircraft up to 1,320 lb, using risk tiers, mandatory detect-and-avoid, Remote ID and UTM traffic integration. The FAA published the proposed rule (NPRM) on August 7, 2025, drew over 3,000 comments, then reopened the comment period on January 28, 2026 (it closed in February). A final rule was widely expected in spring 2026 but has slipped: as of July 2026 it is NOT yet published in final form, and implementation is expected 6-12 months after it is. This is the single biggest lever for US commercial drone growth, and it is still stuck in the pipeline.
heroes.founding_story: The push to 'normalize' BVLOS traces to the FAA's 2021 BVLOS Aviation Rulemaking Committee (ARC) report, after years of one-off waivers and Section 44807 exemptions granted to Amazon, Zipline and Wing created mounting pressure for a real rule. It was turbocharged by President Trump's June 2025 executive order 'Unleashing American Drone Dominance,' which directed the FAA to finally publish a BVLOS rule on a deadline — a deadline the agency has now blown.
heroes.who_should_use: Drone-delivery operators, utility/rail/pipeline/energy inspection firms, precision-agriculture services, public-safety DFR programs, surveyors and mapping companies — essentially every commercial operator whose economics depend on flying past what a human eye can see.
heroes.who_should_buy: This is a rule, not a product — there is nothing to purchase. For operators: do not wait. Get your Part 107, build your safety case and detect-and-avoid plan now, and watch the docket, because those ready on day one will have a real first-mover edge. Who should ignore it entirely: pure recreational hobbyists — recreational flying under existing rules is unaffected.
heroes.free_alternatives: There is no substitute for the rule itself. The available path today is Part 107 plus BVLOS waivers and 44807 exemptions — slow and case-by-case, but real and usable right now. Operators outside the US can look at Europe's U-space framework, but it does not transfer to US airspace.
heroes.verdict: WATCH — the most consequential thing in US commercial drones, but it is still only a proposal; plan and prepare for it, do not bet your launch date on it.

heroes.headline: Ukraine's $1,000 Interceptor Drones Are Downing Shaheds — and the Pentagon Wants In
heroes.one_liner: Fiber-optic 'unjammable' FPVs and $1,000 computer-vision Shahed-hunters are reshaping the war — and the Pentagon now wants to buy them.
heroes.story: Two cheap innovations from Ukraine are rewriting drone warfare. Fiber-optic FPV drones trail a physical spool of cable 30-65 km, making them immune to jamming, spoofing or interception — an upgrade that adds only about $60 per drone, with newer models adding a radio fallback for when the cable snaps. On the defensive side, low-cost interceptor drones like SkyFall's P1-SUN — roughly $1,000 each, ~280 mph, with computer vision and thermal imaging — are claimed to have downed more than 1,500 Shahed loitering munitions and 1,000 other drones in four months. In March 2026 the Pentagon signaled it wants to buy Ukrainian-style $1,000 interceptors, a fraction of the cost of the missiles currently used against cheap drones.
heroes.founding_story: This is a distributed, wartime ecosystem, not a single company — thousands of Ukrainian volunteer workshops, startups and state programs (such as Brave1) iterating weekly since Russia's 2022 invasion. SkyFall is one of the more prominent Ukrainian makers behind the interceptor push; other fiber-optic and interceptor designs come from a shifting roster of small manufacturers. Precise founding details for individual makers are often deliberately obscured for security reasons and are not reliably public.
heroes.who_should_use: Militaries and defense planners studying attritable, low-cost air defense and jam-proof strike; counter-UAS units; and analysts tracking how a $1,000 drone can defeat a multi-hundred-thousand-dollar threat.
heroes.who_should_buy: Not a consumer or investable product — these are battlefield weapons made under wartime conditions, not retail goods, and there is no stock to buy. What is genuinely important here is the doctrine: cost-per-kill is now the decisive metric, and the US is racing to catch up. Who should NOT treat this as actionable: anyone hoping to purchase, invest in, or replicate these systems as a civilian.
heroes.free_alternatives: None applicable — there is no legal civilian equivalent to a loitering-munition interceptor. Hobbyists interested in the underlying tech can legally experiment with fiber-optic video links and computer-vision tracking on sub-250g drones using open-source autopilots (ArduPilot, PX4), which is where a lot of this innovation originated.
heroes.verdict: WATCH — the clearest signal of where warfare is heading and a genuine Pentagon priority, but there is nothing here to buy or invest in.

heroes.headline: Meta's $299 Smart Glasses Ditch the Ray-Ban Logo to Undercut Everyone
heroes.one_liner: Meta's own-brand AI glasses start at $299 with the same camera and chip as Ray-Ban Meta, no logo tax and no display.
heroes.story: On June 23, 2026, Meta and eyewear giant EssilorLuxottica launched a self-branded Meta Glasses line starting at $299, with the Fury and Adventurer frames at $299 and a $399 Starfire edition co-designed with Kylie Jenner. They drop the Ray-Ban and Oakley names but keep the same Snapdragon AR1 Gen 1 chip, 12MP camera, six-mic array and roughly eight-hour battery as the second-generation Ray-Ban Meta. There is no in-lens display here, so you talk to Meta AI and capture photos and video rather than see a screen. They are available now at Meta.com, Best Buy, Amazon, LensCrafters and Sunglass Hut.
heroes.founding_story: Meta's glasses program began with 2021's Ray-Ban Stories, a flop hurt by weak battery life and privacy backlash. The 2023 second-generation Ray-Ban Meta was the surprise hit that pushed camera glasses into the mainstream, built through Meta's multi-year partnership with EssilorLuxottica, the owner of Ray-Ban and Oakley. This 2026 launch is the first time Meta has sold glasses under its own name rather than a fashion house's, a deliberate move to strip out the brand premium and chase volume. Mark Zuckerberg has repeatedly framed glasses as the computing platform that follows the smartphone.
heroes.who_should_use: Commuters and parents who want hands-free photos and video of a moment without pulling out a phone; travelers who want live translation and look-and-ask visual search; POV creators and podcasters capturing first-person clips; and people already living in Instagram and WhatsApp who want quick voice capture on their face.
heroes.who_should_buy: At $299 this is the best-value entry into competent AI camera glasses for someone who mainly wants a good camera, open-ear audio and Meta AI. What is genuinely special is the price-to-hardware ratio: you get essentially Ray-Ban Meta internals for $80 to $100 less. It is otherwise incremental, using the same chip and camera as the 2023 to 2025 models, so existing Ray-Ban Meta owners gain nothing. Do NOT buy if you expected a heads-up display (that is the $799 Ray-Ban Display), if an always-ready camera on your face makes you or the people around you uncomfortable, or if you do not use Meta's apps.
heroes.free_alternatives: The phone in your pocket already takes better photos and does translation and AI queries for free, so the glasses only win on hands-free convenience. Rival camera glasses are worse or gone: Amazon's Bee is audio-only and the old Ray-Ban Stories are discontinued. The real step-up is Meta's own $799 Ray-Ban Display if you actually want a screen. No cheaper glasses match this feature set today.
heroes.verdict: BUY — BUY - The cheapest route into genuinely useful AI camera glasses, but only if you do not already own Ray-Ban Meta and can live without a display.

heroes.headline: Samsung's July 22 Unpacked Promises 'A New Shape' - Galaxy Z Fold 8 and Flip 8 Incoming
heroes.one_liner: Samsung confirmed a July 22 Unpacked for the Galaxy Z Fold 8, Flip 8 and new Watches; the teaser hints at a wider, thinner fold.
heroes.story: Samsung has officially set Galaxy Unpacked for July 22, 2026, at 9 a.m. EDT from London, under the tagline 'A New Shape Unfolds.' Expected on stage are the Galaxy Z Fold 8, a rumored Z Fold 8 Ultra, the clamshell Z Flip 8, and new Galaxy Watch 9 and Watch Ultra 2 wearables, with leaks pointing to a shorter, wider Fold. Nothing is official until the 22nd, so every spec and price is still leak-based. As of July 8 you can register interest for reservation credits but cannot yet buy anything.
heroes.founding_story: Samsung shipped the first modern foldable, the Galaxy Fold, in 2019 after a bruising false start in which review units broke, then recovered to define the category. The Z Fold and Z Flip lines have iterated every year since 2020, leaning on Samsung Display, the in-house panel arm that also supplies rivals including Apple. Unpacked is Samsung's twice-yearly flagship stage, and the summer edition has centered on foldables since 2021. The 'A New Shape Unfolds' teaser hints at the biggest form-factor change to the Fold in years.
heroes.who_should_use: Android power users who want a tablet-sized screen that folds into a pocket; heavy multitaskers running split-screen apps and documents; Flip buyers who want a compact, style-first phone; and Samsung loyalists overdue to upgrade from a Fold 5, Fold 6 or older.
heroes.who_should_buy: Nobody should buy yet. Wait for the July 22 reveal and independent reviews. If the leaks hold, the Fold 8 is for people who genuinely use the large inner screen for reading, docs and multitasking and can stomach a likely $1,800-plus price. What could make it special is a thinner, wider book design with a smaller crease; if it is only a spec bump, it is incremental. Do NOT preorder blind on reservation hype, and do NOT buy a foldable if you do not actually need a folding screen, since a $1,000 slab flagship is more durable and better value.
heroes.free_alternatives: A standard Galaxy S26 Ultra or a Pixel 10 Pro does 95% of what most people need for far less money. Rival foldables already ship and may undercut or out-spec Samsung, so cross-shop the Pixel 10 Pro Fold, Honor Magic V and OnePlus Open. There is no free alternative to a foldable; the honest alternative is simply not buying one.
heroes.verdict: WATCH — WATCH - A confirmed and potentially major redesign, but wait for the July 22 reveal and real reviews before spending foldable money.

heroes.headline: Valve's Steam Machine Is Finally Here at $1,049 - 6x a Steam Deck, But RAM Prices Stung
heroes.one_liner: Valve's living-room SteamOS console-PC shipped June 30 at $1,049; it is powerful and tinker-free, but memory shortages pushed the price up.
heroes.story: Valve's second-generation Steam Machine, a small cube-shaped PC that runs SteamOS on your TV, began shipping June 30, 2026 at $1,049 for 512GB and $1,349 for 2TB, sold through a randomized reservation queue meant to blunt scalpers. Valve says it is roughly six times more powerful than a Steam Deck, built on a semi-custom AMD Zen 4 CPU and RDNA 3 GPU and targeting 4K 60fps with FSR upscaling. It launches alongside a redesigned Steam Controller and the still-unpriced Steam Frame VR headset. Reviewers call it the best plug-and-play living-room PC, but note the price climbed well above early expectations because of the 2025 to 2026 memory shortage.
heroes.founding_story: Valve was founded in 1996 by former Microsoft engineers Gabe Newell and Mike Harrington and runs Steam, the dominant PC game store. Its first Steam Machines in 2015 were third-party PCs running an immature SteamOS, and they flopped badly. Valve regrouped, and the 2022 Steam Deck handheld proved SteamOS and the Proton compatibility layer could run Windows games on Linux at scale. Announced November 12, 2025, this Steam Machine is Valve's own console-like box and its mature second attempt at the living-room dream.
heroes.who_should_use: PC gamers who want console simplicity in the living room without building or tuning a rig; Steam Deck owners who want a big-screen home base that shares the same library; people who dislike Windows overhead and want a quiet, small SteamOS box; and tinkerers who still want an open platform under the hood.
heroes.who_should_buy: Worth it for players with large Steam libraries who want 4K/60-ish gaming on a TV and value SteamOS's simplicity over a Windows gaming PC. What is special is the polish: reservation fairness, a proper controller and a one-tap Steam experience. But at $1,049 and up it is not a value play, since a comparable Windows mini-PC or a PS5 Pro can match or beat it on price per frame. Do NOT buy if you are on a budget, only play a handful of console exclusives, or already own a capable gaming PC.
heroes.free_alternatives: If you already own a gaming PC, Steam Link streams to your TV for free and SteamOS is a free download for existing hardware. Consoles like the PS5 and Xbox Series X are cheaper upfront and get exclusives, and a DIY mini-PC can undercut it. The Steam Machine wins only on the combination of power, small size and SteamOS convenience, not on raw value.
heroes.verdict: WATCH — WATCH - Genuinely the best living-room SteamOS box, but memory-shortage pricing makes it hard to recommend over a cheaper mini-PC or console right now.

heroes.headline: Apple's First Foldable iPhone Is Reportedly Entering Production - for About $2,000 This Fall
heroes.one_liner: Apple's long-rumored folding iPhone is tipped for a September launch above $2,000: crease-free and iPad-style, but still unconfirmed by Apple.
heroes.story: Multiple credible supply-chain reports say Apple's first foldable iPhone, nicknamed the iPhone Fold or iPhone Ultra, is entering mass production around mid-2026 for a September launch beside the iPhone 18 Pro. heroes.headline: curl declares a 'Summer of Bliss': no security reports accepted for all of July
heroes.one_liner: The small team behind code on 20B+ devices will refuse every vulnerability report July 1-Aug 3, 2026 - a burnout flare after an AI-slop era.
heroes.story: curl is the ubiquitous open-source data-transfer tool and libcurl library that runs on an estimated 20+ billion devices - phones, cars, TVs, routers and nearly every backend. On June 15, 2026, lead maintainer Daniel Stenberg announced that the project will not accept or process any vulnerability report between July 1 and August 3, 2026, nicknaming it the 'summer of bliss'; both the HackerOne submission form and the security email address become dead ends for the month. The trigger is exhaustion: the small, volunteer-heavy team had been under intense pressure for months - including a single release that shipped eighteen CVE fixes - on top of the 2025-26 wave of AI-generated 'slop' reports that gutted signal-to-noise, with genuine reports falling from roughly one-in-six to one-in-twenty. As a direct side effect, the curl 8.22.0 release was pushed out to September 2, 2026.
heroes.founding_story: curl was created by Daniel Stenberg in 1996 (first as 'httpget', then 'urlget', then curl) and grew into foundational internet plumbing maintained by a very small core team. The backdrop is real and documented on Stenberg's own blog and Mastodon: curl ran a HackerOne bug bounty from 2019, but in early 2026 it was overwhelmed by confidently-wrong, LLM-fabricated vulnerability reports; the July 2026 blackout is the maintainers collectively taking a break rather than burning out entirely.
heroes.who_should_use: Effectively everyone already depends on curl/libcurl - it is embedded in countless devices and backends. The people who must actually act on this news are security researchers and pentesters (hold your reports until August 3, 2026) and engineering leaders who should note the release slip and plan around no security fixes shipping during July.
heroes.who_should_buy: curl is free and open source under the permissive curl license - there is nothing to buy, ever. If it is load-bearing in your product, the honest cost you owe is support: commercial curl support contracts are available through wolfSSL (Stenberg's employer), and sponsoring the project or its maintainers directly is the actual remedy for the burnout this story is about.
heroes.free_alternatives: For the tool itself, wget handles simple downloads, HTTPie is a friendlier JSON/CLI client, and every language ships an HTTP library - but none match libcurl's protocol breadth or ubiquity, so 'replacing curl' misses the point. The real lesson of this story: there is no free substitute for funded, rested maintainers.
heroes.verdict: USE — USE (and fund) - keep using curl, respect the July blackout, and if it is in your stack, sponsor it; this is the clearest proof yet that critical open source needs money and rest, not just GitHub stars.

heroes.founding_story: MiniMax is a Shanghai-based AI company (backed by Alibaba and Tencent) known for its earlier 'abab' models and the Hailuo video generator. heroes.who_should_use: Teams building coding agents or long-context pipelines (whole-repo reasoning, large-document RAG) who want frontier-ish capability without per-token API lock-in, and researchers who need open weights to fine-tune or audit. heroes.who_should_buy: The weights are free (a permissive MIT/Apache-class license). The real cost is compute: a 428B MoE needs serious multi-GPU hardware to self-host, so most users will either rent a host or use MiniMax's paid API. Using the hosted API is fine for prototyping, but note the governance issue - as a Chinese-company endpoint it is subject to China's National Intelligence Law, so for sensitive data, self-hosting the open weights (or using a Western host) is the honest recommendation.
heroes.free_alternatives: Against closed APIs (GPT-5.5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Claude Opus), M3 trades some quality for open weights and lower cost. Among open-weight peers it is a crowded field: Kimi K2.7-Code for coding-token efficiency, DeepSeek V4 for price and reasoning, Qwen 3.6 for single-GPU practicality, and GLM-5.2. If you need max context plus multimodal in one open model, M3 is compelling; if you just want the best open coder per dollar, benchmark it against Kimi and DeepSeek on your own tasks first.
heroes.verdict: WATCH — WATCH (leaning USE) - genuinely valuable open weights, but wait for independent benchmarks before trusting the 'beats GPT-5.5' framing, and mind the data-jurisdiction issue if you use the hosted API instead of self-hosting.

heroes.headline: mcpsnoop, 'Wireshark for MCP', hits Hacker News as agent debugging matures
heroes.one_liner: A zero-config, single-binary Go proxy that shows every real tool call between your AI client and your MCP servers, live in your terminal.
heroes.story: mcpsnoop, published July 4, 2026 and posted as a Show HN, is a transparent proxy that sits in the real data path between an AI client (Cursor, Claude Code, Codex) and its Model Context Protocol servers, copying every JSON-RPC frame to a live terminal UI while forwarding traffic untouched. Its pitch: the official MCP Inspector connects as its own client, so it never sees what your actual client sends - mcpsnoop shows the real traffic, including the call the model got wrong or never made. It is a single Go binary with prebuilt cross-platform releases, and it adds session replay, capability-negotiation views, latency/error call-outs, stream filtering, and JSON/HTML/text export. As MCP becomes the default way to wire tools into agents, this fills a real debugging gap.
heroes.founding_story: mcpsnoop is an independent open-source project by GitHub developer 'kerlenton,' launched directly as a Show HN on July 4, 2026. It is early-stage with no visible company or funding behind it, so while the tool is immediately useful, treat long-term maintenance as unproven.
heroes.who_should_use: Anyone building or debugging MCP servers or agent integrations: server authors verifying their tools actually behave, and developers chasing down why an agent calls a tool with the wrong arguments (or not at all). Concretely, drop it between Claude Code/Cursor and your server, reproduce the bug, and watch the real frames, latencies and errors.
heroes.who_should_buy: Free and open source; nothing to buy, no cloud tier, no API cost. It runs locally as one binary - the only real 'cost' is trust: it can see all MCP traffic, so review the source before pointing it at anything sensitive.
heroes.free_alternatives: The official MCP Inspector is the obvious free comparison - great for poking a server directly, but by design it cannot see your real client's traffic, which is exactly mcpsnoop's niche. Generic tools like mitmproxy or Wireshark work at the transport layer but are not MCP-aware. For live, MCP-native pipe visibility, mcpsnoop is currently the best free option.
heroes.verdict: USE — USE - if you touch MCP at all, it is a free, low-risk addition to your debugging kit; just remember it is a brand-new solo project, so do not build critical process around it yet.

heroes.founding_story: Emdash is a Y Combinator Winter 2026 company, founded by Arne Strickmann and Raban von Spiegel in San Francisco. The project is young - the repo shows heavy, active development (dozens of releases) rather than a long track record - and deeper origin details beyond the YC batch and founders are not yet publicly documented.
heroes.who_should_use: Developers who already lean on coding agents and want to parallelize - running several agents on separate tickets, or racing multiple solutions to the same bug, with clean worktree isolation. It is a strong fit for teams with issue-driven workflows (Linear/Jira to agent to PR) who want to keep their preferred agent CLI but manage many at once.
heroes.who_should_buy: The app is free and open source; you run it on your own machine. The real costs are downstream: each underlying agent needs its own API key or subscription (Claude Code, Codex, etc.), and running many in parallel multiplies token spend fast - that is the budget line to watch. There is no required paid Emdash cloud tier; remote-over-SSH just uses your own box.
heroes.free_alternatives: Against hosted, paid orchestration (cloud 'agent farm' products or one-shot services like Broccoli), Emdash's edge is being free, local and provider-agnostic. Open-source peers include Conductor-style worktree managers or rolling your own git worktrees plus tmux, and Aider/OpenHands for single-agent flows. If you specifically want a polished multi-agent, multi-provider cockpit, Emdash is the strongest free pick today; if you only ever run one agent, a plain CLI is simpler.
heroes.verdict: USE — USE - the best free way right now to herd multiple coding agents with clean worktree isolation; just watch the combined API bill, because parallelism multiplies token cost.

heroes.headline: ParadeDB pushes 'one Postgres instead of a second search system' as Postgres eats search
heroes.one_liner: Open-source pg_search extension adds Elastic-quality full-text search and vector retrieval to Postgres - 700K+ installs, VC-backed.
heroes.story: ParadeDB is an open-source Postgres extension (pg_search) that adds Elasticsearch-quality full-text search, vector retrieval and fast aggregations directly to a Postgres database - the pitch is 'search without a second system,' so you drop the operational pain of syncing data into a separate Elastic cluster. The ParadeDB Community edition has been installed 700,000+ times, and the project is a standard-bearer for the 2026 trend of Postgres absorbing workloads that used to need dedicated infrastructure. It is used in production from startups to enterprises, including Alibaba Cloud, Bilt Rewards and Modern Treasury. (Its headline funding - a $12M Series A led by Craft Ventures, about $14M total, with Y Combinator participating - landed in mid-2025; the continued adoption through 2026 is the ongoing story.)
heroes.founding_story: ParadeDB is a Y Combinator-backed company created to build a modern Elasticsearch alternative on top of Postgres rather than as yet another standalone search engine. It launched in late 2023 and grew quickly on the back of developer frustration with deploying and syncing separate Elastic/OpenSearch clusters, later raising a $12M Series A led by Craft Ventures in 2025. (Specific founder names are not verified here.)
heroes.who_should_use: Teams already running Postgres who need real full-text search, hybrid keyword-plus-vector search, or analytics but do not want to stand up and sync a separate Elasticsearch/OpenSearch cluster. Concretely: app developers adding search to an existing Postgres app, and teams building RAG or hybrid-search features who want one system for both relational data and retrieval.
heroes.who_should_buy: The Community edition is free and open source and you can self-host it on your own Postgres. Paid options exist - ParadeDB Enterprise (self-managed, for high-availability and large-scale deployments) and managed offerings - and they are worth it mainly if you need enterprise support, HA and scale guarantees rather than DIY. For most teams, self-hosting the free extension is the right start; pay only when uptime and support SLAs justify it.
heroes.free_alternatives: As a replacement for paid/managed Elastic (Elastic Cloud) or OpenSearch, ParadeDB's advantage is not running a second system at all. Other free/open options: native Postgres full-text search plus pgvector (simpler, but weaker relevance and analytics than pg_search), self-hosted OpenSearch or Elasticsearch (more powerful search, far more ops overhead), or Typesense/Meilisearch for lightweight standalone search. If your data already lives in Postgres, ParadeDB is usually the least-effort strong option; if you need heavyweight, tunable search at massive scale, a dedicated engine may still win.
heroes.verdict: USE — USE - if you are on Postgres and tempted to bolt on Elasticsearch, try ParadeDB first; it kills an entire syncing/ops headache for free, and you can pay for a managed tier later only if scale demands it.

all_news.headline: SpaceX's $85.7B IPO: The Biggest Stock Debut in History Is Now Trading
all_news.one_liner: SpaceX (SPCX) raised a record ~$85.7B on June 12, popped 19% day one, then spiked toward $225 and a brief $3T-plus market cap.
all_news.verdict: WATCH — WATCH - Historic and exciting, but a freshly public, wildly volatile mega-cap; let the hype and lockups settle first. Not financial advice.

all_news.headline: Nvidia Is the 'Black Sheep' of the Chip Rally - Up Just ~3% While Peers Soar
all_news.one_liner: The world's most valuable company (~$4.8T) is nearly flat in 2026 as AMD (+171%) and Micron (+305%) rip - the AI leader has become the laggard.
all_news.verdict: WATCH — WATCH - The unusual case of the sector king as the contrarian pick; fundamentally strong but its momentum is broken. Not financial advice.

all_news.headline: Micron's $1 Trillion Moonshot: Up 700% as the AI Memory Shortage Rages
all_news.one_liner: Boise's Micron (MU) hit $1T faster than any company ever and trades near $1,090 - HBM is sold out to 2027 as DRAM prices spike.
all_news.verdict: WATCH — WATCH - The supercycle is real, but so is the cycle; do not chase a 700% move into peak cyclical margins. Not financial advice.

all_news.headline: AMD Is Up 171% in 2026 With the MI400 Launch Near - The Credible Nvidia Challenger
all_news.one_liner: AMD (~$540) has ripped 171% YTD on AI-accelerator hopes; its 2nm MI400 ships in H2 2026 as data-center GPU revenue is seen doubling.
all_news.source_name: S&P Global, 24/7 Wall St., Yahoo Finance
all_news.verdict: WATCH — WATCH - A genuine challenger with a real catalyst, but priced for perfection after a 171% run. Not financial advice.

all_news.headline: Broadcom's AI Revenue More Than Doubles to $10.8B as the Custom-Chip Bet Pays Off
all_news.one_liner: AVGO's custom XPUs for Google, Meta, OpenAI and Anthropic pushed AI revenue to $10.8B in Q2, and it reaffirms $100B+ AI guidance - yet sits ~24% off its high.

all_news.headline: 'Big Short' Michael Burry Bets Against the AI Boom - Shorts Nvidia, Tesla, Caterpillar
all_news.one_liner: Burry has disclosed shorts on Nvidia, Tesla, Caterpillar, Applied Materials and the SOXX ETF; the Shiller P/E near 40 echoes the dot-com peak.

all_news.headline: OpenAI and Anthropic File Confidentially - but May Delay After SpaceX's Rocky Debut
all_news.one_liner: OpenAI filed confidentially (reported ~$730-850B target) and Anthropic followed; both may slip toward 2027 as investors digest SpaceX's wild post-IPO swings.
all_news.source_name: Barchart/The Globe and Mail, AI Weekly

all_news.headline: Figma, a 2025 IPO Darling, Is Down ~40% in 2026 - a Cautionary IPO Tale
all_news.one_liner: Figma (FIG) trades near $21, off its ~$143 peak, hit by lockup expirations and a SaaS multiple reset - a reminder that first-day IPO pops often fade.

all_news.headline: Chip Stocks Slide ~5% on DeepSeek Chip Report - but Nvidia Bucks the Drop
all_news.one_liner: The VanEck Semiconductor ETF fell about 5% on July 7 after a Reuters report that DeepSeek is developing its own AI chip; Nvidia still closed higher.

all_news.headline: curl declares a 'Summer of Bliss': no security reports accepted for all of July
all_news.one_liner: The small team behind code on 20B+ devices will refuse every vulnerability report July 1-Aug 3, 2026 - a burnout flare after an AI-slop era.
all_news.verdict: USE — USE (and fund) - keep using curl, respect the July blackout, and if it is in your stack, sponsor it; this is the clearest proof yet that critical open source needs money and rest, not just GitHub stars.

all_news.headline: MiniMax M3 puts frontier-class, million-token, multimodal model weights in the open
all_news.one_liner: China's MiniMax open-sourced a 428B-param MoE with 1M-token context and native multimodality; it claims 59% on SWE-bench Pro - self-reported.
all_news.verdict: WATCH — WATCH (leaning USE) - genuinely valuable open weights, but wait for independent benchmarks before trusting the 'beats GPT-5.5' framing, and mind the data-jurisdiction issue if you use the hosted API instead of self-hosting.

all_news.headline: mcpsnoop, 'Wireshark for MCP', hits Hacker News as agent debugging matures
all_news.one_liner: A zero-config, single-binary Go proxy that shows every real tool call between your AI client and your MCP servers, live in your terminal.
all_news.verdict: USE — USE - if you touch MCP at all, it is a free, low-risk addition to your debugging kit; just remember it is a brand-new solo project, so do not build critical process around it yet.

all_news.headline: Emdash lets you run a whole team of coding agents in parallel, each in its own worktree
all_news.one_liner: Open-source 'agentic development environment' (YC W26) runs many coding agents at once - Claude Code, Codex, Gemini - isolated in git worktrees.
all_news.verdict: USE — USE - the best free way right now to herd multiple coding agents with clean worktree isolation; just watch the combined API bill, because parallelism multiplies token cost.

all_news.headline: ParadeDB pushes 'one Postgres instead of a second search system' as Postgres eats search
all_news.one_liner: Open-source pg_search extension adds Elastic-quality full-text search and vector retrieval to Postgres - 700K+ installs, VC-backed.
all_news.verdict: USE — USE - if you are on Postgres and tempted to bolt on Elasticsearch, try ParadeDB first; it kills an entire syncing/ops headache for free, and you can pay for a managed tier later only if scale demands it.

all_news.headline: Moonshot ships Kimi K2.7-Code, an open-weight coding specialist tuned for cheaper agent runs
all_news.one_liner: June 12 release: a 1T-param MoE (32B active) with 256K context and roughly 30% fewer reasoning tokens than K2.6, weights on Hugging Face under a Modified MIT license.

all_news.headline: OpenClaw crosses ~382k stars - passing React and Linux - even as security researchers raise alarms
all_news.one_liner: Peter Steinberger's self-hosted personal AI agent is now the most-starred software repo on GitHub, but a self-modifying agent wired to your messengers draws prompt-injection warnings.

all_news.headline: Google's Universal Commerce Protocol advances an open standard for agentic shopping
all_news.one_liner: Google-led open protocol (with Shopify, Etsy, Target, Walmart and 20+ partners) for AI-agent commerce; a March 2026 update added cart and catalog support, and it interoperates with MCP and A2A.

all_news.headline: Google joins the Eclipse Foundation and sponsors Open VSX
all_news.one_liner: Google becomes an Eclipse Strategic Member and backs Open VSX - the vendor-neutral VS Code extension registry (300M+ monthly downloads) behind Cursor, Windsurf, Kiro and Antigravity.
all_news.source_name: Google Open Source Blog / The New Stack

all_news.headline: DeepSeek V4 resets the open-weight cost floor with Pro and Flash variants
all_news.one_liner: The April 2026 open-weight release leans on low price and algorithmic reasoning, leading several competitive-programming benchmarks; weights are on Hugging Face.
